opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really good question, because Facebook ads are one of the honest baselines here. If you want to know whether people will click on something, you can put it in front of real people and measure it. That's real behavior, and I don't think simulation should pretend to replace it.

But I see a few places where simulation adds something ads can't.

The first is the kind of question you can ask. An ad test tells you about a click, a very thin slice of behavior at one moment. Many of the questions people care about are richer than that. How will someone use this product over weeks? How will it change the way they interact with their family, their coworkers, their community? What happens when a whole group adopts it and starts influencing each other? You can't run that as an A/B test on an ad. With generative agents, you can try to model those longer-horizon, social, interactive dynamics, which is what interested me from the start with projects like Smallville.

The second is the cost of being wrong, and the ethics. Some things you shouldn't test on real people first. If you're designing a social platform, a policy, or an intervention that could cause harm, it would be good to explore the space of outcomes before exposing actual humans to it. Simulation gives you a sandbox where failure is cheap and nobody gets hurt.

The third is iteration speed and breadth. Even ad tests take time, money, and audience access, and you can only try so many variants. In simulation, you can explore many more what-if scenarios. What if this group responds differently? What if we change the framing? What if the context shifts? That lets you narrow down which ideas are worth taking to real people.

I'd frame it as complementary rather than either-or. Simulation is where you explore, build intuition, and catch problems early. Real-world testing like ads or field studies is where you ground-truth. And we hold ourselves to that. In our work simulating real individuals, we compared agents' responses against how the actual people answered surveys and experiments, and measured how well they matched. The value of simulation depends on that kind of validation. Without it, it's just a story generator.

So the short answer: ads tell you what people click today. Simulation, done carefully and validated, can help you reason about the richer, social, longer-term behavior that ads can't capture, especially when testing on real people would be too slow, too expensive, or too risky.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation can explore more scenarios and variants, but does not say it can use a larger experimental population than Facebook.

r002.rationale: It does not identify selective participation in online experiments or unrepresentative samples.

r003.rationale: It mentions audience access as a constraint, but does not present access to the desired population—rather than deciding what to ask—as a central research bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It describes modeling longer-term effects and how group adoption can change interactions among families, coworkers, and communities, beyond consumers’ initial reactions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that's actually a really important question, and I want to be careful here, because I don't think the answer is that simulation replaces something like a Facebook ad test. The way I think about it is that those two things are answering fundamentally different kinds of questions.

A Facebook ad test is great if you already know what you want to ask. You have a concept, you put it in front of real people, you see who clicks. It's cheap, it's real behavior, and I would never tell someone not to do that. But it's also very narrow. You get a click-through rate. You don't really get the "why." You don't get to ask the person, "What would make you not use this?" or "What happens six months in when you're bored of it?" And you can't easily iterate. If you want to try fifty variations of a concept, or change the pricing, or see how it interacts with a feature you haven't built yet, each of those is a new campaign, a new budget, a new week.

Where I think simulation becomes valuable is upstream of that. It's the part of the process where you don't even know what the right question is yet. You can take a population of simulated agents that are grounded in real people, real interview data, and you can have a conversation with them. You can run a thousand little experiments in an afternoon that you'd never be able to justify running in the real world, just to find the two or three that are actually worth spending real money on. So in a sense, simulation is how you figure out which Facebook ad to run.

The other thing I'd say is that the ad test only tells you about the people who happen to be on Facebook, in the demographic you targeted, in the moment they're scrolling. A simulation lets you reason about populations that are hard to reach, or situations that haven't happened yet. That's where I think the generative part really matters: you're not just measuring, you're exploring.

Now, the honest caveat is that simulation is only as good as how faithfully it reflects real people, and that's the thing we spend most of our time worrying about. If the agents aren't grounded, you'll just get confident-sounding nonsense. So I'd never say trust the simulation over the real test. I'd say use the simulation to be much smarter about what you test for real.

r001.rationale: It says simulation can run many experiments and reason about hard-to-reach populations, but does not state that its experimental populations can be larger than those available through Facebook.

r002.rationale: It notes that Facebook ad results reflect the people targeted and the moment they are scrolling, but does not identify selective participation in online experiments as a source of unrepresentative samples.

r003.rationale: The response frames not knowing what question to ask as a central reason to use simulation. It does not identify access to the desired population, rather than deciding what to ask, as customers’ central research bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It describes using simulation to explore what happens six months later and how a product feature or pricing change interacts with behavior, beyond consumers’ initial reactions.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re useful at different stages. With Facebook ads, you’re getting a real behavioral signal: someone saw this message and clicked on it, or they didn’t. If that’s the question you’re trying to answer, there’s a lot of value in observing actual people.

The opportunity with simulation is to explore possibilities before you decide which ones to test. You might have twenty different product concepts, or you might want to understand how a concept would play out in a social setting, where people influence one another. Simulation could help you narrow that space and generate hypotheses that you then take into a real-world experiment.

But the important caveat is that a simulation isn’t automatically a reliable model of people just because it produces believable behavior. You have to validate it for the particular question you’re asking. So I see it as a complement to something like Facebook ads: a way to help decide what to test, with real human behavior still providing the check.

r001.rationale: It mentions exploring twenty product concepts, but does not say simulation can use experimental populations larger than Facebook can reach.

r002.rationale: It does not identify selective participation or unrepresentative samples in online experiments.

r003.rationale: It does not describe access to the desired population as a central customer research bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It says simulation can explore how a product concept plays out socially, where people influence one another, beyond measuring an individual's initial click reaction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Facebook ads are a great way to test whether people respond to a particular message or concept. You’re putting something in front of real people and observing what they do. I wouldn’t view simulation as a replacement for that.

Where simulation could be useful is earlier in the process, when you’re still exploring what to build and why different people might care about it. You can ask follow-up questions, vary the scenario, and explore how a product might fit into someone’s life. That can help you develop better hypotheses before you run a real-world experiment.

There’s also a distinction between an individual response and a social process. An ad might tell you whether someone clicks, but you might want to understand how people discuss a product, influence one another, or develop norms around using it. Simulation gives you a way to explore those interactions. The key is to validate whether the simulated behavior actually predicts the behavior you care about. Otherwise, you have an interesting story, but not necessarily useful evidence.
